The International Court of Justice (ICJ) will rule on whether Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, in a judgment that could see the court hold a state responsible for genocide for the first time.
Officials announced on Tuesday that the court's president, Judge Yuji Iwasawa, would read the judgment at a public sitting at the Peace Palace in The Hague at 10am local time on 19 November.
The ruling will be final and binding, with no right of appeal.
Several governments have already described the violence as genocide, including the US and Canada.
Legal experts say they expect the outcome to have consequences for other ICJ cases involving allegations of genocide, most pressingly South Africa's case against Israel over its war against Palestinians in Gaza, where the confirmed death toll has reached almost 75,000 people.
The case, brought by the Gambia in 2019, concerns the Myanmar military's 2017 violence in Rakhine State, which drove more than 700,000 Rohingya into neighbouring Bangladesh and involved widely documented massacres and rapes.
About 1.2 million Rohingya, a predominantly Muslim minority, now live in camps around Cox's Bazar, the world's largest refugee settlement.
Myanmar has denied committing genocide, saying its forces were responding to insurgents from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (Arsa), whose attacks on police posts in August 2017 killed 12 security personnel.

Israeli politicians and commentators have accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of attempting a coup after his election defeat last week, which followed a historic turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel.
They say he is using the Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic intelligence agency, to undermine the result and retain power.
More than a week after the results showed the Netanyahu-led bloc trailing the opposition, Shin Bet chief David Zini is reportedly leading investigations into the Palestinian vote. The inquiries have raised allegations of voting fraud, bribery and foreign interference, despite no evidence being made public.
The investigations coincide with Netanyahu’s campaign to delegitimise the Palestinian-led parties Ra’am and the Joint List, which together secured an unprecedented 19 seats in the Knesset. Critics say the effort is aimed at keeping him in power.
On Tuesday, the Shin Bet arrested Middle East Eye contributor Abd Abu Shahadeh, citing a “security-related investigation”. Israeli media reported that Zini also wants Palestinian political leaders Ahmad Tibi, Sami Abou Shahadeh, Mansour Abbas and Ayman Odeh questioned.
Yair Golan, leader of the opposition Democrats party, warned on Wednesday that Israeli democracy was under threat.
“The police are detaining political activists without a warrant. The Shin Bet is trying to question senior elected officials without presenting evidence. The outgoing government refuses to recognise the election results,” he said.
Golan later accused Netanyahu of trying to “carry out a coup and seize power by force”.

A German court has rejected applications by defence lawyers to hear expert witnesses in an ongoing trial of five activists alleged to have broken into an Israeli-owned arms factory.
Daniel Tatlow-Devally, Zo Hailu, Crow Tricks, Vi Kovarbasic and Leandra Rollo, who are from Germany, Spain, Ireland and the UK, were arrested on 8 September following an alleged break-in on the premises of Israeli arms firm Elbit Systems in the southwestern German city of Ulm.
Known as the “Ulm Five”, the group is accused of damaging the building's glass facade and smashing office equipment, including computers, screens and telephones.
They have been held for over a year in pretrial detention.
Defence lawyers told Middle East Eye that the court has either not responded to or rejected applications to hear from expert witnesses who could give testimony on the arms company’s role in Israel’s genocide in Gaza.
The legal team resorted to presenting two witnesses in person, as, under German law, a court is obliged to hear evidence from witnesses summoned by the defence if they filed an application to do so.
However, the court can reject the application if it deems the evidence to be inadmissible.
On 14 October the defence presented weapons expert Dr Shir Hever, who could speak about the connection between the technology developed at the Ulm site and Israel’s onslaught on Gaza.
After a day of deliberations the judge rejected the application, on the basis that the software developed at the laboratory had no connection with Israel’s offensive in Gaza.

It took nine months, but regime change has finally been achieved.
Nine months after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Mossad director David Barnea put the idea into US President Donald Trump’s head that regime change was possible, it has been achieved.
The only variation on the plan that all three men worked on is that regime change has happened in Texas, Michigan, Kansas, Georgia, Florida, and in Congress - not in Tehran.
The war on Iran is the defining mistake of Trump’s second term as president, and of Netanyahu’s final term of office - but Iran is by no means their sole nemesis.
For the president who knew nothing about Iran, it was more than a bet that went sour. The fact that it was all Netanyahu’s idea makes failure even worse for the leader of an “America First” movement. Iran is a quintessentially “foreign war” that proved the principle on which Trump himself campaigned.
Failure in Iran was different for the prime minister who had the Islamic Republic in his sights for most of his adult life.
It was a classic example of military and intelligence overreach. Netanyahu and Mossad thought they could do to a whole country what they thought they had done to two movements: Hamas and Hezbollah. They totally underestimated the power of the Islamic Republic to resist.
But war on Iran, and the economic disaster it unleashed on both sides of the Gulf and beyond - including record prices at gas stations - are not the real cause of the earthquake that has shaken US politics.

The Democrats secured a sweeping midterm election victory on Tuesday, but one critical question remains unresolved: is US President Donald Trump now more or less likely to resume the war on Iran with the election cycle over?
Before the midterms, the US appeared to be on the verge of launching a new, wide-scale attack against Iran.
The families of US diplomats were evacuated from the region, and additional US military assets flooded into the Middle East. Arab leaders issued cryptic warnings about a devastating new conflict.
But the attack many diplomats and analysts expected around election day never materialised. In fact, Republicans are now blaming the Iran war, and even Israel, for their blistering defeat at the hands of the Democrats.
Trump said on Wednesday that "it's largely true" the Iran war and high fuel prices tied to the conflict led to his party’s historic defeat.

Egyptian-American surgeon Adam Hamawy has won his bid for Congress in New Jersey’s 12th congressional district, joining the blue wave across the US and making history as the first Muslim and Egyptian American to represent the state.

Republicans previously held the majority of the House of Representatives with 218 seats, four more than the Democrats at 215, but come January, Hamawy is one of the congressional wins to give his party a majority. with a whopping projected 250 seats, according to MS Now.

“I'm a surgeon, and I can tell you that we are going to stop the bleeding. We are going to fight for every American that's been left behind by the establishment that has been ruling Washington for so long.”

Israel is at risk of internal collapse or civil war because of tensions among Israelis, an August report by CIA experts tasked with providing “alternative analysis” said, according to a report by Drop Site News published on Monday.
The CIA report, titled “Fracture From Within", said that Israel faces a volatile situation ahead of 27 October elections, where Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will be fighting for his political future.
The authors noted that one of the most divisive Israeli political issues is the long-standing exemption from military service that ultra-Orthodox Israelis enjoy.
The row has exposed deep divisions within Netanyahu's right-wing bloc and raised questions about whether he will have the support of two ultra-Orthodox parties: United Torah Judaism (UTJ) and Shas - his most dependable allies since he first became prime minister in 1996.
While hundreds of thousands of reservists have been mobilised for Israel’s genocide in Gaza and wars on Lebanon, Syria and Iran, ultra-Orthodox men have historically been exempt from compulsory military service in order to pursue full-time religious studies in yeshivas.
The arrangement has long been contentious, but the war has intensified pressure to end the exemption.
Netanyahu's coalition has repeatedly failed to pass legislation regulating ultra-Orthodox enlistment, leading to the detention of dozens of young men accused of evading military service and triggering mass protests backed by UTJ and Shas.

Speaking at a high-profile space conference attended by diplomats and space agency representatives, Erdogan called for the cosmos to remain peaceful for scientific exploration rather than the next arena of military conflict.
"Sending weapons to space, or turning space into a ground for an arms race, will be totally wrong," Erdogan told the International Astronautical Conference (IAC) in Antalya, southern Turkey on Monday.
"It will be a direct threat to the joint future for humanity, and I see that this race is becoming widespread - which, of course, we do not welcome."
Erdogan is the first Nato leader to issue a condemnation of space weapons after the United States last month publicly acknowledged for the first time that it had deployed a space weapon into Earth’s orbit.

The father of an Israeli man killed by Israeli military fire during the Hamas-led attack of 7 October 2023 has branded Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a "traitor", and told him: "You did not protect my son."

“It’s a disgrace that you didn’t protect those murdered on October 7,” Yaakov Godo shouted out. “The blood of my son and of another 1,200 people murdered in a single day is on his (Netanyahu's) hands and on his head.”
Netanyahu briefly interrupted his speech. "I wanted to tell him he was a traitor - but I couldn't," Godo said afterwards.
“I managed to stand up to him once. I don't have many opportunities to meet him. It was important to me to tell him that the blood of my son and the blood of 1,200 other people murdered in one day - it's on his hands and on his head," the bereaved father continued.
"He never turned to talk to us. No one came to us and no one even informed us that Tom was killed. Only the army came after a year and a half and said that it was sorry and that Tom was shot by army soldiers,” Godo said.

Turkey supplied anti-drone air defence systems to Ukraine earlier this year, allowing Kyiv to test new products and bolster its capabilities, several people familiar with the matter told Middle East Eye.
The sources said Ukraine had imported a small number of Turkish-made Korkut air defence systems, which typically consist of three weapon system vehicles and one command-and-control vehicle. They declined to disclose how many units had been deployed on the battlefield.
Produced by Aselsan, Korkut uses air defence guns to shoot down aerial targets, including the cruise missiles and drones that have become a persistent threat in the war in Ukraine. The system is designed to counter first-person-view and tethered drones using 25-millimetre smart ammunition.

When I sat down with Mothin Ali early on Sunday, he was in an energetic mood.
It was the third and final day of what must have been an arduous Green Party conference for its co-deputy leader, who was dressed in his usual suit and flat cap.
"It's been a fantastic year," Ali beamed. "We had 400 councillors elected in May, 1,300 councillors in all, a fifth MP in parliament and our membership has quadrupled.
"It's a phenomenal record so far."
The Greens surged in the polls last year after Polanski was elected leader. They gained further momentum and credibility with a by-election victory in Gorton and Denton in February and then took more votes from Labour in the May local elections than Reform did.
Polanski is at least partially responsible for Keir Starmer's downfall and Andy Burnham's premiership. On Friday evening the renowned political analyst John Curtice argued as much at a packed fringe event.
The conference in the sunny seaside town of Brighton was full of energy. For many members it was the event of the year: Friends roved the conference in groups and went off to restaurants and bars in the evening. They were diverse in age and ethnicity; many wore keffiyehs and Palestine badges.

Israel shells Syria's Quneitra while Qatar and Jordan condemn its excavation near occupied Golan
Israeli forces shelled farmland between Buraiqa and Kodana in southern Quneitra, Syria's Al-Ikhbariah TV reported on Sunday.
Meanwhile, Syria, Qatar and Jordan denounced Israel's resumed construction on the "Sofa 53" project in Syria's Quneitra province.
The project, also called the "Great Storm", is a military road that Israel began building in 2022 within the buffer zone established under the 1974 disengagement agreement.
It stretches from northern Quneitra down towards the meeting point of the Syrian, Jordanian and Israeli borders.
Syria's Foreign Ministry said on Sunday that Israel's resumption of excavation work near the separation line with the occupied Syrian Golan Heights was a "flagrant breach" of the 1974 deal.
Qatar also described the project as a violation of Syrian sovereignty and international law and a threat to stability in the region.
Jordan expressed similar condemnation, with foreign ministry spokesperson Fuad Majali urging Israel to stop all actions targeting Syria.

Israeli opposition leader Avigdor Lieberman on Sunday called for the Palestinian Authority (PA) to be dismantled and for an Israeli-Jordanian confederation to control parts of the West Bank currently under the PA's control, according to Haaretz.
Lieberman, chairman of the right-wing Yisrael Beiteinu party, presented a plan titled "Israel's Endgame in the West Bank and Gaza".
Under it, Israel would apply sovereignty over Area C, which makes up about 60 percent of the occupied West Bank and remains under full Israeli control.
The plan proposes an Israeli-Jordanian confederation in Areas A and B, where the PA exercises limited control.
Jordan would run civilian affairs and policing there, while Israel would keep "full security responsibility" across the entire territory, according to Lieberman's plan.
He also called for control of the Gaza Strip to be handed to an "external party", which he did not specify.
Under international law, the entire territory covering Areas A, B and C is Palestinian land and all Israeli settlements on them are illegal. The vast majority of Israel’s 700,000 settlers live illegally in Area C.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday ordered a security review of international flights to Israel after a co-pilot allegedly attempted to crash an Israel-bound flight from Dubai.
Netanyahu "has instructed the Head of the National Security Council, Shmuel Ben Ezra, to appoint an examiner to conduct a thorough review of all security aspects of foreign civil aviation to Israel", a statement from his office said.
The Israel-bound Flydubai flight made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on 30 September after its Omani co-pilot allegedly attempted to crash the plane, which was carrying 180 passengers, most of them Israeli.
Netanyahu said on Friday that Israel was examining whether anyone had directed the co-pilot, vowing a "heavy price" for those involved.
A source close to the UAE government accused the Israeli government of exploiting the incident for political purposes, Israeli media reported on Saturday.

Iran airlines resume flights to Iraq’s Najaf after US exemption
Iranian airlines resumed flights to Iraq’s Najaf on Sunday after the United States granted Baghdad an exemption allowing sanctioned Iranian carriers to operate to the city holy to Shia Muslims, AFP reported.
On Friday, the Iraqi government said it had secured an agreement with the US allowing Iranian airlines, except Mahan Air, to operate 40 daily flights to and from Najaf.
Last month, Iraq enforced the US ban on Iranian carriers, especially at Najaf’s airport, which is a major hub for Iranian flights.
The US also granted Iraqi Airways, the national carrier, a waiver to fly between Najaf and Iran, with the flights expected to start this month.
